1: Welcome to Module 12 of the Non-Person Identity learning path: migrate a service account, from a user account to a G M S A, a D M S A or Microsoft Entra.
It teaches the companion guide Service Accounts, with Chapters 6 and 5 of the developer workbook.
The module takes about sixty-five minutes, with a lab on fixtures and a lab for a test domain.
2: A service account's password is the one nobody changes, because changing it breaks something.
Modules 7 and 8 taught the kit's plans for converting those accounts.
This module takes one account at a time and walks it through each move by hand, with Microsoft Learn's own commands, so you know what the plans send before you approve one.

There are three moves: a user account to a group managed service account, the same account to a Windows Server 2025 delegated managed service account, and an account to a Microsoft Entra workload identity, once the workload moves or gains a cloud path.
Then you watch the kit plan the same moves on fixtures.
The module adds no gate of its own: its moves are Gate G5's, and its rules are the track's.
3: Here's what you'll be able to do by the end of this module.
You'll compare the kinds of service identity: who holds the credential, where it runs and how exposed it is to Kerberoasting.
You'll choose a target with the guide's decision path, and name its Chapter 3 disposition.
You'll follow Learn's steps to a G M S A and to a D M S A, with the checks before the switch and the rollback after it.
You'll say what moves to Microsoft Entra I D, what can't, and why a hybrid workload keeps both.
And you'll match each step to the kit's plan action, which runs only by its approved hash and never deletes.
Take Module 3 first, for the dispositions.
Module 8 is recommended: this module reruns part of its lab.
4: Unit 1 starts with the guide's comparison table.
Read it for two things: who manages each credential, and which kinds speak Kerberos.
A user account used as a service has a password an administrator sets by hand, and it's highly exposed to Kerberoasting when it holds an S P N.
An S M S A and a G M S A have a long random password that Windows manages; a G M S A's is computed by the domain controllers from the K D S root key, and any host allowed to retrieve it holds it.
A D M S A binds the secret to the machine, and Microsoft Learn says it's designed against Kerberoasting.
The Microsoft Entra kinds, a managed identity, an app registration with a certificate and a federated credential, speak OAuth, not Kerberos.
So the table makes two things plain.
Nothing in Microsoft Entra I D speaks Kerberos for a service.
And a G M S A is a better password, not a different protocol.
5: Next in Unit 1 is the decision path.
Answer questions one to eight in order; the first yes is the target, and each target lines up with a Chapter 3 disposition.
An account that's disabled, unused or without an owner is retired.

A workload on Azure gets a managed identity; one in CI/CD gets a federated credential; one on premises that calls Graph gets the Arc identity or a certificate, and if it also needs Kerberos, it goes on to question five as well and takes two dispositions.

An account that's already a G M S A or D M S A is kept, and one that must stay a traditional account, because the service supports no managed account or relies on unconstrained delegation, is kept on Kerberos; each with an end date.
Then a traditional account that needs Kerberos, with a Windows Server 2025 domain controller and every host on 2025, gets a D M S A.

Any other case that needs Kerberos, a standalone account included, gets a G M S A. Question nine applies to every target from five to eight: Kerberos to a resource with no Entra equivalent also puts it on the island list.

Then the track's rules, which a hand migration follows too: two named owners and a sponsor; a reviewed disposition first; a thirty-day parallel run, then disable, and never delete during the migration; no client secrets; no privileged groups; and changes that are reviewed.
6: Unit 2 is Migrations A and B, by hand.
In Migration A, a user account to a G M S A, watch for the order.
There's one K D S root key for the forest, and the domain controllers wait up to ten hours from its creation before they allow a G M S A to be created.
Then you create the G M S A, install it and test it on every host.
Then you switch the workload and move the S P N's in one change window.
After a clean thirty days in parallel, the old account is disabled and moved.
Migration B, a user account to a D M S A, starts with Learn's limits: every machine that uses the account must support D M S A.
Then you create, start, wait and complete.
Learn says to wait at least two ticket lifetimes; the program's thirty days covers four.
Learn's D M S A page says never to delete the original account.
Then skim the guide's special cases, and stop on failover clusters and Microsoft Entra Domain Services.
7: Unit 3 is Migration C, from Active Directory to a Microsoft Entra workload identity.
It starts when the workload moves to Azure, or gains a call to Graph or an Azure A P I, and only for what it reaches with OAuth.

Learn's order of preference for an app's credential is a managed identity whenever possible; federation where the app doesn't run on Azure; otherwise a certificate from a trusted certificate authority, kept in a vault; and never a client secret.
The guide has four targets, C1 to C4, and step C5 retires the on-premises account after the parallel run.
Learn has no Entra identity a service can use for Kerberos or N T L M to an on-premises resource.
A workload that reaches a file share, a sequel Server login mapped to a Windows account, or a Kerberos-only application that way keeps its G M S A or D M S A until that resource changes.
That's why a hybrid workload keeps both.
8: Lab 1 reruns parts of the workbook's Chapter 6 and Chapter 5 labs, in PowerShell 7, in the non-person identity folder.
The domain and tenant are fictional, nothing signs in, and nothing is sent.
Step one makes the runs Chapter 6 reads: Chapter 1's register, Chapter 2's owners and Chapter 3's dispositions.
It prints nothing, and no account moves without its disposition.
Step two runs Learn's G M S A, D M S A and K D S steps against stand-ins: seventeen tests, each a fact about one of Learn's published procedures.
B1 skips Learn's delegated M S A state step, because it fails as published.
B2 restarts only the service that uses the account, where Learn's step restarts every running service.
A3 adds A E S two fifty-six, which Learn's G M S A sample leaves out.
A4 is a person's step on each host.
And A7 disables the old account, where Learn's Entra page deletes it.
9: Step three checks the Kerberos accounts and builds the plan.
The plan has ten actions, five of them writes: one D M S A completion, two G M S A creations and two retriever changes.
One write is a person's and four are the pipeline's, and nothing is sent.
Note the plan's S H A two fifty-six on the last line: it's what someone approves.
Look first at K D S root key Ready.
The check reads the key's start time, with a delegated read, and it never creates a key.
Learn's K D S page says the forest needs one root key, and the guide says to create only one.
10: Step four reads the two migrations the plan sends.

Create G M S A, for S V C dash intranet, is the guide's step A3 under the managed service account standard: a name, its D N S host name, the service-account O U, its one domain local group of hosts as the retrievers, A E S two fifty-six, and the thirty-day interval stated at creation.
It isn't outbound-only, because it takes over S V C dash intranet's S P N's.
Complete D M S A migration, for S V C dash H R sync, is step B3, with the D M S A and the superseded account's distinguished name.
Its migration started forty days before, more than the program's thirty.
11: Step five dry-runs the plan with its approved hash, as the pipeline.
This is the program's rule that changes are reviewed: the write path sends only a plan whose S H A two fifty-six was approved.
The pipeline's G M S A would send the G M S A creations and the retriever changes.
The D M S A's completion, step B3, needs Domain Admins, so it's a person's step, and the pipeline refuses it.
M S A dash print oh one is an S M S A, so it goes to a G M S A, never to a D M S A.
12: Step six builds Chapter 5's conversion plan: that's Migration C. Step seven reads what each conversion replaces, and its parallel run.
There are five Active Directory accounts and three client secrets, each going to a managed identity, a federated credential or a certificate, and the plan holds each to Learn's order of preference.
Conversion six gives an Azure Functions app a certificate where a managed identity is available, so Chapter 5 flags it.
Conversion one has run forty days on its user-assigned managed identity, so its old account shows ready to disable.
That row exercises the parallel run only: the program's target for S V C dash H R sync is a D M S A, the completion in step four, so don't take it through step C5.
Conversion eight's old secret still signs in on day fifty-nine, so it stays.
13: Lab 2 does the moves for real, in a test domain, never production.
By hand, for one account: the guide's Migration A, steps A1 to A7, with Learn's commands and the expected output after each one.
You need a test domain with a K D S root key older than ten hours, a test user account with an S P N, and a member server that runs a test service as it.
Back out with the guide's rollback for Migration A.
Or through the kit: the workbook's Chapter 6 Lab 2.

It makes a traditional test account, a test M S A and the G M S A's domain local retriever group, applies the plan as a person in the test domain, and runs a D M S A migration to completion on a Windows Server 2025 domain.
Its step six backs it out.
14: The guide's evidence table has a row for every step, and these are the rows this module practices, in nist special publication eight hundred fifty-three.

Creating the account supports A C six, Least Privilege, I A five, Authenticator Management, and C M three, Configuration Change Control, with the approved plan, its SailPoint request and ServiceNow change, and the apply manifest.
Installing and testing supports A C six, with Test A D Service Account true on each host.
The parallel run supports A C two, enhancement three, Disable Accounts.
The cloud identities support I A nine, Service Identification and Authentication, tailored in.
And the island supports C M eight, System Component Inventory, with Chapter 6's island list.
K S I's are fed-ramp twenty X indicators for cloud service providers, and which file supports which is the program's mapping: design guidance.
15: First: a workload stays on premises and needs Kerberos.
The domain has a Windows Server 2025 domain controller, but one of the two hosts that run the service is on Windows Server 2022.
The answer is b, a G M S A.
A D M S A needs every host that uses it on Windows Server 2025.
Second: Learn's Entra page ends a move to a G M S A by deleting the old account.
It disables the account after a clean thirty-day parallel run, and deletes it only later, through the decommission process.
The program follows the stricter reading.
The module page has three more questions, each linked to the section that answers it.
16: You compared the kinds of service identity, chose targets with the decision path, and read Learn's steps for a user account to a G M S A, a D M S A and a Microsoft Entra workload identity.

Then you saw the kit plan the same moves: a G M S A with the standard's settings, a D M S A migration completed after its parallel run, five Active Directory accounts and three secrets converted in Learn's order of preference, and every plan sent only by its approved hash.

The evidence an I S S O keeps for a migration is the guide's evidence table by step, with the kit's two plans and their approved hashes, the apply manifests, Test A D Service Account on each host, and the island list for what stays.
